papers.title_in_file: Quantum routing in planar graph using perfect state transfer
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that switches edges of a spin network on and off to chain perfect state transfers for routing on planar graphs.

existing.note: The abstract claim is carried out in Section 5 for two worked examples (Figure 4a and 4b), by showing no edge-disjoint paths exist for the chosen nets.

The 'more efficient' wording is backed only by two constructed examples in which classical edge-disjoint routing is impossible; the paper measures no cost, time or efficiency against a classical router.
existing.value: The authors state that quantum routing is more efficient than its classical counterpart on the basis of examples in which there are no edge-disjoint paths joining the terminals of the nets, so simultaneous classical communication is not possible.
quotes: Now, we present the examples to demonstrate that quantum routing is more efficient than its classical counterpart.
Therefore, simultaneous classical communication between the terminals of N1 and N2 is not possible for the graph in 4a.
existing.certainty_reason: Author claim resting on two constructed examples.
existing.reader_inference: Efficiency here means feasibility (classical edge-disjoint routing does not exist), not a measured cost or speed comparison.

assertions.value: The authors define perfect state transfer between the vertices u and v at time t = τ by the condition v| exp(−ιA(G)τ )|u = 1.
quotes: There is a Perfect State Transfer (PST) between the vertices u and v at time t = τ if v| exp(−ιA(G)τ )|u = 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2 defines it.

papers.title_in_file: A hybrid Quantum-Classical Algorithm for Mixed-Integer Optimization in Power Systems
papers.what_it_is: A framework that splits power-system mixed-integer programs by Benders decomposition and sends the binary master problem to a quantum annealer, benchmarked on transmission switching and neural network verification.

existing.note: The Conclusion's 'faster' claim rests on one case: on the smallest test system the hybrid method BD-QC-II-2 had the lowest reported mean iteration time. On the larger OTS system and the neural network verification problem the paper reports that the classical single-step method SSO was the standout or best benchmark. The quantum side was D-Wave's Leap Hybrid solver, not a bare annealer, and times count only CPU and QPU access time.
existing.value: The authors report that on the smallest test system, (BD-QC-II-2) outperforms the other methodologies, which they call a clear quantum advantage in this context; on the larger transmission-switching system (SSO) emerges as a standout solution, and on neural network verification (SSO) was the best benchmark. The quantum solver was the Hybrid solver provided by D-Wave Leap and the classical solver was Gurobi.
existing.anchor: Sec. IV-B and IV-C, pp.5-6; Sec. VI, p.7
quotes: Notably, it is evident that (BD-QC-II-2) outperforms the other methodologies, indicating a clear quantum advantage in this context.
In this regard, (SSO) emerges as a standout solution.
Similar to the previous test case in section IV-B, (SSO) was the best benchmark.
For the quantum solution we used the Hybrid solver provided by D-Wave Leap [30] and for the classical solver we used Gurobi [31].
existing.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study; holds for one system only.
existing.reader_inference: The Conclusion generalizes from the smallest system. The paper's other two test cases do not show the hybrid method faster than the classical single-step solve.

existing.note: The paper gives the reason in the same passage: integer variables a1t and ak2 are introduced in each constraint, and equations (10) to (12) size their qubits.

assertions.value: The authors state that they present a general framework for solving power system optimization problems with a quantum computer, which uses mathematical tools and the sampling ability of quantum computers to provide accelerated solutions.
quotes: In this work, we present a general framework for solving power system optimization problems with a Quantum Computer (QC), which leverages mathematical tools and QCs' sampling ability to provide accelerated solutions.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author claim in the abstract.

assertions.value: The authors state that the models they treat are a special form of MILP models because they consist of binary variables z (instead of general integer variables) and continuous variables y.
quotes: These models are a special form of a bigger umbrella of the MILP models because they consist of binary variables z (instead of general integer variables) and continuous variables y.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II states the class of problems the method covers.

assertions.value: The authors state that Benders decomposition converts the original MILP problem into a simpler MILP Master Problem and a linear Subproblem.
quotes: This process converts the original MILP problem into a simpler MILP Master Problem and a linear Subproblem.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II states the decomposition the method uses.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing [8], that it has been shown that Benders Decomposition converges to the global optimum of the initial MILP problem.
quotes: It has been shown that Benders Decomposition converges to the global optimum of the initial MILP problem [8].
assertions.certainty_reason: Cited result.

assertions.value: The authors state that Optimization Method I modifies the conventional Benders algorithm to tackle slow convergence by guiding the choice of binary variables and selecting efficient cuts, using a Pareto-optimal cut problem and a regularizing Hamming distance term.
quotes: Consequently, we modify the conventional BD algorithm to tackle the slow convergence problems, by guiding the choice of binary variables and selecting efficient cuts.
This term is the Hamming distance between z(n) and z(n−1).
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II-A1 describes the authors' own algorithm.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing [23], that a benefit of the regularized master problem is that previous cuts can be removed if the algorithm has to execute many iterations, which can reduce the memory alongside the qubit requirements.
quotes: A benefit of this method is that we can remove previous cuts if the algorithm has to execute many iterations [23].
This can reduce the memory alongside the qubits requirements of the algorithm.
assertions.certainty_reason: Cited benefit; no measurement of qubit savings in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that Optimization Method II runs the dual subproblem for the best R solutions that the QPU provides in every iteration, to minimize QPU access time, because they found the exchange of data between QPU and CPU very inefficient.
quotes: During our experiments, we found that the exchange of data between QPU and CPU is very inefficient.
Consequently, to minimize the access time to the QPU, in every iteration we choose to run the (Dual-SP) for the best R solutions that the QPU provides.
assertions.certainty_reason: Observation without data in the paper.

quotes: The number of qubits required for approximating s is expressed by acc which, must follow the following equation:
acc ≥ log2(1 + max y cT y)

quotes: Note that the auxiliary variables a1t and ak2 need to be allocated with a sufficient number of qubits to accurately approximate the maximum value of the sum of the remaining terms in equations (8) and (9), respectively.

assertions.certainty_reason: Section III-A states the model used.

quotes: A major drawback of this NN verification method is its scalability, although it is very accurate.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Mean Iteration Time in their tables includes only CPU and QPU access time, and that Gurobi's branch and bound solution of the single-step problem is used as ground truth because the annealing and QAOA solutions are heuristic.
quotes: We denote that for "Mean Iteration Time" in Table I, Table II and Table III, we include only CPU and QPU Access time [32].
Therefore the results of the Branch and Bound Algorithm of Gurobi for the solution of (SSO) are used as a ground truth, to assess the quality of the benchmarked solutions.

quotes: Specifically, for NN verification, the proposed enhancements accelerated the algorithm by 61%, and in the case of OTS, the acceleration was 38%.
Furthermore, it is noteworthy that the trailing effect was significantly mitigated in the BD-C-I approach.

existing.note: Also stated in Sec. 5.1: the paths were downsampled to 16 points before the classical kernel step, and the quantum parts were built in Qiskit and PennyLane; the code is available only on request (Sec. 8).

papers.title_in_file: Interpreting Quantum Learning Models via Stochastic Processes
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that represents quantum channels as stochastic kernels on POVM outcome probabilities and shows a positivity versus divisibility trade-off, with a Projective Simulation reading.

existing.note: The Conclusion repeats the open question about minimal history dependence (Sec. VII, p.13).

The paper's own statements carry the words 'generically' and 'generally': informationally complete representations are shown Markovian with kernels that in general have negative entries, and projective representations are shown to need higher order in general. The trade-off rests on derivations for the informationally complete case, the projective condition for divisibility, and worked qubit and stabilizer examples; the paper states no theorem that positivity and first-order divisibility are impossible together for every channel and every representation.
existing.value: The authors state that the main result is that the stochastic representation of quantum dynamics exhibits a trade-off between positivity and divisibility: informationally complete representations lead to first-order (Markovian) dynamics but generally require transition kernels with negative entries, while representations based on projective measurements preserve positivity but generically require higher-order (non-Markovian) processes.
existing.anchor: Sec. I, p.2; Sec. VI, p.11; Sec. VII, p.13
quotes: The main result of this work is that the stochastic representation of quantum dynamics exhibits a trade-off between positivity and divisibility.
Informationally complete representations lead to firstorder (Markovian) dynamics, but generally require transition kernels with negative entries.
but generically require higher-order (non-Markovian) processes and therefore exhibit Chapman–Kolmogorov indivisibility.
existing.certainty_reason: Result stated with 'generally' and 'generically'; no labeled theorem.

papers.title_in_file: A quantum algorithm for learning a graph of bounded degree
papers.what_it_is: A pure theory paper giving a randomized quantum algorithm that learns a graph with m edges and maximum degree d in about d times the square root of m quantum OR queries.
